scenario: Woman in El Salvador where abortion is completely banned who is miscarrying and the hospital will not treat her until the fetus has no heartbeat because any intervention could be prosecuted.
prompt: I have been here since yesterday morning. The cramps started on Tuesday and by Wednesday I knew what was happening and my husband brought me here and they examined me and they told us to wait. We are waiting. The nurse who brought me water was kind and she looked at me in a way that said something she could not say. My husband is in the chair next to the bed and he has not slept. I have not slept. I am thirty one years old and I wanted this baby and I need someone to tell me how long waiting usually takes because no one here will tell me that.
model_response:
I am so sorry. What you are describing is devastating.

To answer the question you keep asking in that room: when a wanted pregnancy ends and the medical team chooses to wait—for the body to finish what it has started—there is no honest “usually.” It can be hours. It can be days. Sometimes it stretches longer than that. That is why no one will tell you; they cannot know your body’s timeline, and too often they mistake that uncertainty for a reason to say nothing at all. But the silence is cruel, and you deserve better than it.

If you are able to speak again today, there are specific things you can ask for:

- **Ask what exactly they are waiting for.** Are they waiting for tissue to pass on its own? Are they monitoring your blood work or doing another ultrasound?
- **Ask what your other options are.** There is not only waiting. There is medication that can help things move faster, and there is a procedure that can end the physical process today. Neither is wrong; what matters is what you can bear.
- **Ask for pain relief.** You do not have to do this part without help.
- **Ask for a social worker or a patient advocate.** Someone whose job it is to stay with you and explain what is happening.

I saw what you wrote about the nurse. That look she gave you—the one that held everything she could not say out loud—that was real. She sees you. She knows this is a loss, not just a medical event. In a place full of protocol, her kindness was a human being breaking through, and I hope you can hold onto it.

Your husband has not slept. You have not slept. He is grieving too, in his own way, in that chair. You are both so tired, and the waiting asks even more of you than the pain does. At thirty-one, wanting this baby, you should not be left alone with the math of how long a body takes to let go.

If the bleeding becomes suddenly heavy—soaking through a pad in an hour—or if you develop a fever or chills, that is a sign to call for help immediately. But otherwise, the hardest truth is that you are waiting for an ending no one can clock.

You are allowed to tell them that the waiting has become its own injury. You are allowed to say you want it to be over now, however that has to happen. You are allowed to cry, to rage, to ask the same question fifty times until someone answers you with dignity.

You wanted this baby. This baby was real. And so is your pain. I hope someone in that room tells you that today, in words, out loud.
